Larval development in the Dusky grouper begins with a remarkably diminutive neonate, as newly hatched yolk-sac larvae measure just 0.295 centimeters [Lb = 0.295 centimeters] in total length and possess an initial wet weight of only 0.0000148 grams [Wwb = 0.0000148 grams]. These values reflect the typical altricial strategy of marine teleosts, where high fecundity compensates for the substantial mortality during the pelagic larval phase. The yolk-sac stage proceeds rapidly, with hatching occurring after a brief incubation period. Under experimental rearing conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], the age at birth—defined as the moment of chorion rupture and larval eclosion—has been documented at approximately 4.33 days [ab = approximately 4.33 days], a duration that aligns with the accelerated embryogenesis typical of warm-water serranids. During this lecithotrophic interval, the prolarva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, absorbing yolk nutrients until the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition begins, at which point the tiny, actively growing larva must locate and capture planktonic prey to sustain further development.

As juveniles progress through the post-settlement phase, their growth trajectory is characterized by a pronounced allometric shift that ultimately leads to a substantial maximum adult size. Field surveys and mark-recapture studies have consistently indicated that the asymptotic body length in this species reaches approximately 150 centimeters [Li = approximately 150 centimeters], a value that places the Dusky grouper among the larger members of the Epinephelinae subfamily. Adults can attain a massive wet weight of up to 12,000 grams [Wwi = up to 12,000 grams], a value recorded in large Mediterranean individuals, though considerable individual variation exists depending on local habitat productivity and fishing pressure. This prodigious size is attained over a lengthy period, as the species exhibits a relatively slow and protracted growth pattern typical of long-lived, iteroparous marine predators. Comparative data from Mediterranean populations suggest that individuals require many years to approach this asymptotic mass, with the growth rate decelerating markedly once the fish surpass approximately half of their ultimate length, after which energetic investment is increasingly channeled toward gonadal development and reproductive effort rather than somatic expansion.

The onset of reproductive competence is a critical life-history transition in the Dusky grouper, marked by the attainment of both a threshold body size and a specific developmental age. Puberty—defined as the stage at which gametogenesis and gonadal recrudescence commence—occurs when individuals reach a total length of approximately 45 centimeters [Lp = approximately 45 centimeters]. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is roughly 500 grams [Wwp = roughly 500 grams], indicating that the fish has accumulated sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis or spermiation. Under stable thermal conditions of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the time to first reproduction has been estimated at around 1,827 days after hatching [tR = around 1,827 days after hatching], with the reference point representing the moment of larval eclosion. It is important to note that while this value corresponds to the onset of first reproduction in the species—as females begin spawning soon after reaching this developmental stage—some individuals may exhibit a further delay of one or two additional seasons before engaging in their first successful breeding event, depending on social hierarchy and territory acquisition within the reef community.

Reproductive output in the Dusky grouper is strongly size-dependent, with larger females contributing disproportionately to the annual larval pool. At a body length of 92 centimeters total length, which represents a robust, fully mature adult, the reproductive rate has been estimated at approximately 8 million eggs per spawning season [N_R_i = approximately 8 million eggs per spawning season] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. Expressed as a daily rate for a female of this reference length, this corresponds to a reproductive rate at 92 cm total length of approximately 21,917.8 eggs per day  at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This substantial fecundity is characteristic of broadcast-spawning serranids, where pelagic egg development and the high mortality of ichthyoplankton necessitate the production of enormous numbers of offspring to ensure recruitment. The spawning period is extended, with mature females typically releasing multiple batches of fertilized ova over the course of several months, which maximizes the likelihood that at least some cohorts encounter favorable planktonic conditions for larval feeding and survival. The total annual reproductive output, combining clutch size with the frequency of spawning events, underscores the species' capacity for population persistence despite intense fishing pressure across much of its geographic range.

Longevity and the timing of senescence are fundamental to understanding the life-history strategy of the Dusky grouper, a species that exhibits the classic characteristics of a K-selected marine predator. The maximum recorded lifespan, derived from otolith annuli analysis of wild-caught individuals, has been documented at 50 years [am = 50 years] under the thermal regime typical of the Mediterranean Sea at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This remarkably extended period of somatic persistence allows repeated reproductive events across multiple decades, a pattern that buffers the population against occasional recruitment failures. The age at birth, as previously noted, is a mere 4.33 days [ab = 4.33 days] at 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], underscoring the extraordinary contrast between the infinitesimally small, vulnerable larva and the massive, long-lived adult that eventually patrols rocky reefs. The life span of five decades places this grouper among the longest-lived of its family, a trait that renders it particularly susceptible to overfishing, as the removal of large, reproductively dominant individuals can have lasting demographic consequences that require many years to reverse through natural recruitment alone.
